Full text

Abstract

Bilingualism is a multidimensional, dynamic construct that is challenging to measure. Common bilingualism questionnaires differ in the items they contain, complicating comparisons across studies. Prior work has shown limited content overlap between questionnaire items, but the extent of conceptual, or latent overlap between questionnaires remains unclear. We assessed conceptual overlap among seven bilingualism questionnaires by analyzing participant responses rather than questionnaire content. We administered all seven questionnaires to French-English and English-French sequential bilingual undergraduates. Then, we used multiple factor analysis (MFA) to identify latent dimensions capturing shared variance across questionnaires. MFA identified two latent dimensions, corresponding to L2 usage and L2 history/acquisition, which together accounted for 32% of cross-questionnaire variance. MFA also revealed differences in how each questionnaire (and the constituent items) contributed to the global latent dimensions. These findings suggest that the degree of conceptual overlap between questionnaires may be stronger than item analyses imply. While questionnaires should not be seen as directly interchangeable, their convergence suggests that the diverse measures they employ capture shared aspects of bilingual experience.

[div-01]

Bilingualism is multifaceted, changes over time, and varies in quality and quantity of use and exposure across social contexts. In research, characterizing this diverse lived experience quantitatively is challenging. Researchers have devised a wide range of instruments to operationalize and measure bilingual experience (Surrain & Luk, 2019), posing challenges for research synthesis and meta-analytic efforts aimed at understanding the behavioral and neural differences associated with multilingualism (Anderson et al., 2024). Researchers interested in multilingualism have developed different questionnaires to capture this life experience. Over the last two decades, these questionnaires have improved the consistency with which this experience is documented across studies. However, these questionnaires still vary in scope, depth, and focus, leaving open questions about their comparability. It is understandable that researchers may aim to characterize different aspects of multilingualism. However, overlapping measurement, at least at the broad stroke, could facilitate meta-scientific investigation. One important question is: what common characteristics of multilingualism are captured by these questionnaires?

Questionnaires use participant self-report to capture various aspects of bilingual experience. These concepts, stemming from researchers' top-down intuitions about the salient features of bilingual experience, include: age of acquisition, which has implications for how quickly a language can be learned and the types of neuroplastic changes that accompany this learning (Deluca et al., 2019; Luk et al., 2020); exposure, which speaks to qualitative (e.g., types of instruction or media) and quantitative (e.g., degree of immersion) aspects of language experience (Deluca et al., 2019); proficiency, which approximates mastery of a language and is commonly split into four sub-domains of reading, writing, speaking, and listening; patterns of usage, including time spent using given languages, frequency of switching between or mixing languages, and contextual factors like activities (e.g., watching TV, reading the newspaper, or using social media) for which languages are used or people (e.g., parents, siblings, friends, coworkers, etc.) with whom languages are spoken.

Another set of relevant features of bilingual experience relates to personal identity and subjective beliefs and attitudes. While these features are held by individualshttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?Q77xeU they are influenced by the broader ecological and societal contexts surrounding the individual (Titone & Tiv, 2023) , e.g., the social status of a specific language or one's membership in a racial, ethnic, or linguistic minority community. Such values and beliefs inform how individuals use, switch between, or mix their languages (Yim & Clément, 2021). In turn, these beliefs can interact with the features described above, such as frequency of use and proficiency attained.

Lastly, the aforementioned features are all fluid across various timescales (Grosjean, 2010 (Grosjean, , 2016;; Jessner, 2008). Discrete life events, such as moving to a new city or country, starting a new job, or even making new friends, can precipitate changes in language experience. Similarly, language acquisition does not occur in an instant, but usually unfolds over several years. The pace of learning and proficiency attained, as well as the extent of concomitant neural adaptations (Pliatsikas, 2020), depends on the frequency, quality, and duration of sustained exposure and active use. Furthermore, attrition is often a result of reduced exposure and/or usage and results in a decline in proficiency or language control over time (Köpke & Schmid, 2004).

Depending on resources and investigative aims, researchers may choose to capture multilingualism periodically across the lifespan or focus on the period immediately preceding study participation (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?broken=06kY0d Li et al., 2020). This fluidity across time and researchers' focus on either or both timescales add further diversity to multilingual experience.

Questionnaires used by researchers interested in multilingualism appear to be diverse, although there has been limited research on their comparability. Table 1 documents the commonly used questionnaires, their approximate lengths, and the key constructs they are meant to assess. At first glance, these questionnaires seem to examine diverse aspects of multilingualism, as corroborated by two recent studies (Dass et al., 2024; Kašćelan et al., 2022). Kašćelan and colleagues (2022) evaluated questionnaires used to measure bilingualism in children and found that even when questionnaires assess similar constructs, their operationalization can still differ widely. For example, while many questionnaires aim to measure exposure and usage, some ask about both in a single question, while others contain separate items for each construct. Similarly, questionnaires vary with respect to the interlocutors, contexts, and activities about which exposure-and usage-related items are framed. Sincehttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?bQ83vE according to Grosjean's Complementarity Principle (Grosjean, 2016) , individuals use different languages in different contexts and with different people, usage measurements could differ widely depending on the specific operationalization of usage-related questions. Thus, even apparent similarities between questionnaires could lead to divergent research outcomes.

Further evidence of differences between questionnaires comes from Dass et al.'s (2024) content overlap analysis. The authors used a two-level category framework: the first levelhttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?02TSKP derived from top-down concepts identified by Kašćelan et al. (2022) , consisted of six categories (production, switching, exposure, subjective statements, identity, and history/acquisition), and the second level consisted of more detailed descriptors of contexts (e.g., home, school, social media), interlocutors (e.g., friends, parents, strangers), and skills (e.g., reading or writing).

Combining these two levels yielded category labels such as Exposure-home and Production-speaking. Each item in seven bilingualism questionnaires was assigned a category, and content overlap was assessed by comparing the number of categories shared by two questionnaires with the total number of categories in each questionnaire. Perfect overlap between two questionnaires would result in a Jaccard Index of 1, while no overlap would result in a Jaccard Index of 0. The average overlap between questionnaire pairs was 0.16, and the highest overlap between two questionnaires was 0.30, suggesting weak overlap between questionnaires.

The practical implications of these item-level differences between questionnaires remain unclear. On one hand, these differences could mean that different questionnaires tap into different underlying constructs and are therefore not interchangeable or comparable. However, it is also possible that, despite differences in item categories or wordings, questionnaires nevertheless measure the same (or similar) underlying constructs, i.e., they load on similar latent variables. If the latter is the case, focusing too much on the overlap, or lack thereof, of questionnaires at the item level risks discarding the diversity across questionnaires as noise rather than treating it as signal. Building on previous work on assessing the tools characterizing multilingualism, we aim to (1) evaluate the conceptual overlap between common bilingualism questionnaires accounting for nuanced differences between questionnaire items; and (2) determine whether shared items across questionnaires are answered consistently.

To achieve these aims, we used a multivariate, data-driven approach to determine the extent of conceptual overlap among bilingualism questionnaires administered to the same participants. Crucially, this analysis centered on participants' responses to different questionnaires on the same information, which is not expected to differ. We administered seven common bilingualism questionnaires to a large sample of French-English bilingual undergraduate students located in the Ottawa area. Then, we applied multiple factor analysis (MFA; Abdi et al., 2013) to the questionnaire response data to identify latent dimensions capturing shared variance across questionnaires. We expected that some questionnaires would cluster together, i.e., be similar to one another, while others would deviate given their more specific focus. The extent and nature of conceptual overlap was an exploratory aim. were recruited via the student participation pool in an introductory psychology or cognitive science course at their university and compensated with course credit. To be eligible, participants were expected to be native speakers of English or French (but not of both languages) and at least moderately proficient in the other language. Some participants may have been multilingual, i.e., spoken additional languages besides English and French, but we did not collect data on additional languages. In total, 462 participants completed all seven language questionnaires (see Table 2). The uOttawa sample was split roughly in half between L1 English and L1 French. In contrast, the Carleton sample comprised nearly 90% L1 English speakers. Apart from differences in the proportion of L1 English/French speakers, there were no significant differences in age, gender, or education between sites. Differences in average L2 age of acquisition (AoA) were not significantly different (p = .11), but participants recruited from the uOttawa reported significantly higher proficiency in L2 speaking, listening, reading, and writing than participants from Carleton (p uncorrected < .001). Given that both samples shared a societal context (i.e., attended university in the same city), the samples were combined in our main analyses.

Materials and Procedure

We administered the same seven language questionnaires (see Table 1) examined by Dass et al. (2024). In each questionnaire, we replaced all participant-facing occurrences of 'L1' and 'L2' with the names of each participant's respective languages (either French or English). However, all analyses were conducted using L1/L2 labels. Items concerning additional languages were removed from the LHQ, LEAP-Q, and LSBQ to limit study duration to under an hour.

All data were collected online. Participants accessed the study through their university's recruitment platform. First, they completed an informed consent form. Next, they completed the screening questionnaire to determine their L1 and L2, in order of acquisition, for subsequent language questionnaires. Then, they completed the seven language questionnaires. The questionnaires were presented in a fixed order. Roughly half of the participants (n = 200) were given BLP, BSwQ, BEQ, LEAP-Q, LSBQ, BDS, and LHQ, while the rest (n = 262) had the questionnaires administered in reverse order.

Cleaning and processing questionnaire data

Data from the seven language questionnaires were exported from Qualtrics as numeric codes. Due to experimenter error, more than half of the items from the LHQ were lost. To prepare the data for MFA, we first removed all non-numeric (i.e., open-text) and non-linguistic (i.e., demographic) items, leaving 289 items directly related to language acquisition, use, exposure, and proficiency. We also removed 94 items deemed unfit for multiple factor analysis (see Table 4 for removal criteria and a breakdown by questionnaire), including: 22 items representing unordered factors (e.g., items for which response choices included L1, L2, or both languages); 18 items with more than 20% missing responses (e.g., items related to usage with spouses, which most of our sample left blank); and 54 items with minimal variance (i.e., items for which the most frequent response occurred more than four times more often than the second most frequent response; many of these items related to L1 AoA and proficiency, which were at floor and ceiling, respectively). The remaining 195 items consisted of numeric data (represented as scales, dropdowns, and sliders) and were treated as continuous for subsequent analyses. Note. A subset of language-related questionnaire items was included in the numeric multiple factor analysis. Items representing unordered factors were excluded, as were items with more than 20% missing responses and items with insufficient variance (i.e., the most common response occurred more than 4 times more often than the second most common response).

Variables related to age of acquisition and foreign accent strength were reverse-coded so that higher values indicated a higher degree of bilingualism, enabling interpretation consistent with other language items. Notably, we did not remove items that failed to correlate with other items within their own questionnaire. While this step is common in exploratory factor analysis of single questionnaires (e.g., Anderson et al., 2018), we wanted to ensure that we did not omit items that were unique to their respective questionnaires but related to items from other questionnaires.

Analysis

To assess the quality of questionnaire inputs and the suitability of multiple factor analysis, we computed correlations between groups of items identified as similar across questionnaires. Five items pertaining to L2 Age of Acquisition (see Table 5) and four related to L2 speaking proficiency (see Table 6) were identified manually by researchers, and items related to L2 usage were identified by searching the items for the words 'use' and 'usage' and manually filtering the results.

To assess the level of conceptual overlap between the language questionnaires, we ran multiple factor analysis (MFA; Abdi et al., 2013) using the FactoMineR R package (Husson et al., 2006). This method was intended to identify latent dimensions capturing shared variance across the seven questionnaires. While MFA is conceptually similar to a standard exploratory factor analysis insofar as both methods aim to identify latent dimensions that explain substantial variance (Field et al., 2012), MFA functions mathematically as a 2-step hierarchical principal components analysis (PCA; Abdi et al., 2013). First, PCA is run on each group (in our case, questionnaire) independently. Each PCA yields a set of principal components (and corresponding eigenvalues) describing variance within a single group (i.e., questionnaire). The resulting values are then used to normalize each group's data (by dividing its values by the first singular value, i.e., the square root of the eigenvalue of the first principal component). Normalization ensures that when data from all groups are pooled for further analysis, features such as internal variance and column length (i.e., number of items per questionnaire) will not influence the MFA solution.

In our case, this step prevented a questionnaire like the BSwQ, which contains only questions about switching and should therefore have a prominent first principal component (i.e., one that explains a high degree of observed variance), from dominating more holistic questionnaires that likely have less prominent first principal components because the questionnaires assess additional components relating to multilingualism.

A second, non-normalized PCA is then run on the compromise or consensus, a single table formed by concatenating the normalized group tables from the first PCAs. This second PCA yields a new set of orthogonal principal components (also called dimensions). Each dimension explains a certain amount of cross-group variance, characterized by a percentage and an eigenvalue. A common rule of thumb is to retain dimensions with eigenvalues higher than 1 (Kaiser, 1960). However, eigenvalues and the percentage of variance explained only provide insight into the quantitative extent of overlap between groups.

To understand the qualitative nature of this overlap, dimensions must be interpreted by inspecting their relationships with groups (language questionnaires), columns (questionnaire items), and rows (participants) in the data set. For each dimension, each questionnaire gets a contribution value representing how much variance it explains. Similarly, items also get contribution values for each dimension. Lastly, each participant receives a set of factor scores (one for each dimension) that represent how their individual responses correlate with the variance captured by that dimension. A dimension can be characterized (i.e., labeled by researchers given the research questions) by inspecting the items that contribute most strongly to it. Similarly, the directionality of a factor score can be assessed by comparing responses for contributing items between participants with high and low factor scores.

Results

To assess the extent of conceptual overlap between bilingualism questionnaires, we analyzed participant responses to 195 items across seven questionnaires. First, we assessed three subsets of items-those related to L2 AoA, L2 speaking proficiency, and L2 usage-with univariate correlations to assess the reliability across questionnaires in measuring these three common constructs. These three constructs marked onset age, skill, and functional use, which are common characterizations of multilingualism (Luk, 2015). Then, we assessed all 195 items using multiple factor analysis to identify latent patterns of shared variance between questionnaires.

Correlations between items related to L2 age of acquisition (see Tables 5a and 5b) and self-reported L2 speaking ability (see Tables 6a and 6b) demonstrate a high degree of reliability of these items across questionnaires despite differences in how items are phrased. In contrast, correlations among usage-related items (see Figure 1) suggest greater diversity in how questionnaires operationalize this construct. All correlations were statistically significant in the

L2 AoA and L2 speaking proficiency analyses, as were most correlations between L2 usage items. Nevertheless, correlation values were not uniform: the LSBQ proficiency item correlated more moderately than other proficiency items, and a subset of LSBQ items related to media consumption and social activities correlated more strongly than other usage items.

The MFA identified 5 orthogonal latent dimensions explaining 44.2% of the variance across questionnaires (see Table 7). However, only the first two dimensions met our criteria of having an eigenvalue greater than 1 (Kaiser, 1960) and explaining more than 10% of the overall variance (Field et al., 2012). Exploratory analyses were conducted to determine the effects of questionnaire order and site on the MFA solution. These analyses suggest that the main solution is robust across questionnaire orders and sites, both in terms of questionnaires' loadings on the first two MFA dimensions (see Figures S3 and S4) and the qualitative characterization of the first two dimensions as respectively capturing usage and history/acquisition (see Tables S1 and S2).

The first dimension, explaining just under 21% of the overall variance, was mainly related to language usage (see Table 8). Seven of the top 10 items contributing to this dimension were related to patterns of language usage, including the use of L1/L2 for reading, the use of L2 with friends, and switching or mixing languages.

Higher factor scores corresponded to higher L2 usage and lower L1 usage, whereas lower factor scores corresponded to higher L1 usage and lower L2 usage. Additionally, three proficiency items (speaking, writing, and listening) from the LHQ appeared in the top 10 contributing items to Dimension 1, with higher factor scores corresponding to higher self-reported proficiency. Seventy-eight items, 40% of the total items entered in the analysis, made above-average contributions to this dimension (see Figure S1).

The second dimension, explaining just over 11% of the overall variance, was related to language history and acquisition (see Table 9 and Figure S2). Nine of the top 10 contributing items to this dimension related to L2 age of acquisition (AoA), number of years of childhood schooling in L2, or the age at which participants began speaking, reading, or writing in their L2.

The final item in the top 10 contributors to Dimension 2 related to L2 listening proficiency.

Higher factor scores corresponded to earlier L2 AoA (reverse-coded) and a higher degree of education in L2, and lower factor scores represented later L2 AoA and lower formal L2 education in childhood. A total of 31 questions contributed more than average to this dimension, with three AoA questions from the BLP dominating. Note. The MFA also enabled differentiation of the questionnaires by how well they were represented by each of the first two dimensions (see Figure 2 and Table 10). In the first dimension (usage), five questionnaires (BEQ, BLP, LEAP-Q, LHQ, and LSBQ) were strongly represented, the BSwQ was moderately represented, and the BDS was weakly represented. In contrast, in the second dimension (history/acquisition), the BDS was most strongly represented, followed closely by the LHQ, with the remaining five questionnaires being moderately to weakly represented.

Discussion

We investigated the conceptual overlap between seven commonly used bilingualism questionnaires. Previously (Dass et al., 2024), we examined questionnaire content overlap by categorizing questionnaire items top-down as described by Fried (2017). In the current study, we instead analyzed participant responses to questionnaire items. We identified sets of questions on L2 AoA, proficiency, and usage, and observed moderate-to-high correlations among participant responses within these sets. Then, using multiple factor analysis, we identified two latent dimensions that captured a moderate amount of shared variance across the questionnaires, indicating partial conceptual overlap. However, large residual variance suggests that, despite considerable conceptual similarity, no two questionnaires are equivalent.

Correlation analysis supports the assumption of reliability between questionnaires in measuring well-known constructs. For L2 AoA and L2 proficiency, items across questionnaires correlated strongly, indicating high reliability. Nevertheless, the strength of these correlations varied, and this variance likely reflects subtle differences in question wording (see Tables 5 and 6). For AoA, the highest correlation (0.86) was observed between LSBQ and BDS items, both of which ask the participant the age at which they learned their L2. In contrast, the lowest correlation (0.69) was observed between the LSBQ and BLP items, the latter of which asks participants when they started learning their L2. For L2 speaking proficiency, items from the LEAP-Q, BLP, and LSBQ all correlated strongly (i.e., above 0.7) with each other, with the LSBQ item having relatively lower correlations (i.e., 0.4 -0.5) with other items. The relative outlier status of the LSBQ item could be due to its stipulation, absent from the other three questionnaires, that the participant compare their proficiency to that of a native speaker.

For items related to L2 usage (see Figure 1), a range of correlations illustrated greater diversity in how questionnaires operationalize this construct compared to AoA and proficiency.

Nevertheless, the majority of correlations observed were both positive and significant, indicating consistency in L2 usage behaviors across contexts within individuals. One region of the correlation matrix with particularly high correlations is the section of LSBQ items related to specific activities: with the exception of praying, the surveyed activities (e.g., social media, reading, and extracurriculars) exhibited highly correlated patterns of L2 usage. Conversely, the three LSBQ items related to early childhood L2 exposure (infancy, preschool, and primary school) exhibited nonsignificant or significantly negative correlations with items related to present L2 usage. Similar data should be collected from other samples to determine the generalizability of these trends.

Taken together, the three correlation analyses indicate that questionnaires operationalize AoA, proficiency, and usage constructs similarly but not identically. These differences may result from subtle differences in item wordings that, in turn, influence participant responses. Thus, when comparing two studies that incorporate these constructs but measure them with different questionnaires, it is crucial to consider how closely the respective questionnaires and their constituent items operationalize the relevant constructs. These considerations can be made at the item level or at a more conceptual level, i.e., that of the overarching aims of the questionnaires.

Multiple factor analysis (MFA) provided quantitative and qualitative insight into the conceptual overlap between questionnaires. Our MFA identified two latent dimensions that together accounted for 32% of the cross-questionnaire variance, indicating moderate conceptual overlap between the questionnaires. Inspection of how individual items contributed to each latent dimension enabled qualitative characterization of this overlap. While it is important to acknowledge that latent dimension may not map perfectly onto a priori concepts, we nevertheless observed a strong relationship between the first two latent dimensions and the commonly studied constructs of usage and history/acquisition.

Nearly all items contributing to the Dimension 1 were related to L2 usage, with a large number of items (78, 40% of total items) contributing more than average to this dimension and no items dominating the contribution (see Table 8). These findings echo those of the correlation analysis: given the high proportion of usage questions and the moderate correlations among many usage items, it is perhaps unsurprising that usage emerged at the core of the first latent variable accounting for the most shared variance across questionnaires.

The second dimension, L2 history/acquisition, is dominated by a smaller set of L2 AoA items (see Table 9). The top three contributors, all from the BLP, probe different aspects of acquisition: the age at which the participant learned their L2, the age at which the participant became comfortable speaking their L2, and the number of years of schooling the participant had in their L2. The strong contributions from these items suggest that they capture distinct aspects of L2 acquisition, an ongoing process that may differ among individuals in terms of onset, learning rate, exposure, and use.

Proficiency items appeared in qualitative characterizations of both dimensions, reflecting the deeply interrelated nature of proficiency to other aspects of language experience. One proficiency item appeared in the top 10 contributors to Dimension 2 (history/acquisition), underscoring the deep interrelatedness of language history/acquisition and proficiency that has been observed in samples of immigrants immersed in monolingual societies (Mechelli et al., 2004). Similarly, three proficiency items appeared in the top 10 contributors to Dimension 1 (usage). The contribution of the same proficiency item (L2 listening proficiency) to both orthogonal dimensions suggests that early acquisition (Dimension 2) and recent usage (Dimension 1) constitute distinct paths to proficiency.

Multiple factor analysis also enabled more granular comparisons of questionnaires in terms of how strongly each questionnaire loads on the two latent dimensions (see Figure 2). Five questionnaires (BEQ, BLP, LHQ, LSBQ, and LEAP-Q) have roughly equivalent loadings on the usage dimensions, suggesting they capture usage to a similar extent. In contrast, the BDS and LHQ load more strongly on the history/acquisition dimensions than other questionnaires. When considering both usage and history, the LHQ best captured these two dimensions holistically (see Table 10). Among the questionnaires, the LSBQ and BEQ are most similar in the strength of their representation on both the usage and history dimensions. When selecting an instrument, researchers should thus consider, in addition to more practical constraints such as questionnaire length and cost of administration, which latent dimensions matter most to their research questions and hypotheses.

One set of limitations of the present study stems from our focus on sequential speakers of French and English. Our inclusion criteria were kept narrow to facilitate numeric factor analysis and maximize the detection of a stable dimension structure in a moderate sample size. These criteria enabled us to present questionnaire items using concrete languages (English and French) but to score them easily in terms of L1/L2. In turn, we were able to conduct one analysis with both French-English and English-French bilinguals. However, this choice comes with limitations to generalizability: it is unclear whether our two-dimension structure would replicate in simultaneous bilinguals, who arguably have more than one L1; with other language pairs besides French and English; or multilinguals, i.e., individuals speaking three or more languages.

Furthermore, we do not know how many of our participants may have been multilingual. Future research conducted outside the Ottawa context and including more diverse samples, other language pairs, or a generalized multilingual approach could improve on the generalizability of our findings.

Concerns about generalizability also apply to the multiple-factor analysis approach. In general, factor analysis solutions are only intended to describe the samples from which they are derived (Field et al., 2012), and the validity of applying an existing solution to a new sample depends on the degree of similarity between the new sample and the original. While MFA is, strictly speaking, a hierarchical principal component analysis and not a type of factor analysis, concerns about generalizability are still warranted. Nevertheless, the stability of our dimensional structure across questionnaire order (see Figure S3; Tables S1 and S2) and educational institutions (see Figure S4; Tables S1 and S2) suggests that the MFA approach may prove robust across more diverse contexts.

The decision to use numeric MFA, which requires numeric or ordered factorial inputs, led to a relatively poor representation of the BDS in our analysis. Three of the original 11 language items in the BDS, including items about language use at home and for mental arithmetic, were unordered factors. These items were removed, along with five items about L1 that had near-zero variance, leaving only three items for inclusion in the MFA. The limited representation of the BDS may have contributed to its low loading on the Usage dimension. Future studies may benefit from employing mixed MFA analysis or qualitative techniques to allow for inclusion of unordered factor inputs, such as questions that ask participants to choose between the unordered options of "L1", "L2", or "both languages".

Another limitation stems from the present study's focus on self-report measures and the lack of objective measures of language proficiency and dominance. In contrast with self-report measures, instruments such as the Multi-Lingual Naming Test (Gollan et al., 2012) and the Boston Naming Test (Kaplan et al., 2001) measure proficiency objectively based on language task performance. Self-report measures have been shown to correlate with objective measures of language performance (Luk & Bialystok, 2013; Marian et al., 2007). As a result, self-report measures are often used as convenient proxies of more logistically challenging objective measures. Howeverhttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?fdKk2F the correlation between subjective and objective measures varies depending on the specific feature of bilingualism being investigated (Sheng et al.https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?JvR9gP 2014) , participants' degree of bilingualism (Botes et al., 2026) , and external factors such as cultural norms and the degree of bilingualism in participants' environments (Tomoschuk et al., 2019). Importantly, the choice between self-report and objective measures has been shown to influence the outcomes of studies linking language to cognition (Botes et al., 2026). Work extending the present study should include objective measures alongside self-report measures to determine which self-report item variants are the most reliable proxies for objective measures and to better understand the relationship between objective measures and latent dimensions identified by multiple factor analysis.

While this study identified three items from the BDS that capture disproportionately high variance in the Acquisition/History dimension, we do not make strong recommendations regarding the items' utility in the context of research on cognition. An important consideration for selecting items (or latent dimensions derived from them) is their predictive utility, which can only be determined on the basis of their relation to cognitive measures of interest, e.g., executive function or attention. Future work should investigate differences between questionnaire items and latent dimensions in predicting behavior to motivate recommendations for further standardizing the operationalization of bilingualism.

In conclusion, we demonstrated that commonly used bilingualism questionnaires capture overlapping, but non-identical, facets of bilingual experience. By examining participant responses to questionnaire items, we observed broad item-level convergence, despite minor differences, between sets of items deemed similar a priori. Furthermore, we identified two latent dimensions, relating to usage and history/acquisition, that captured 33% of shared variance across questionnaires. Taken together, these findings indicate partial conceptual overlap between questionnaires. While the residual variance suggests that no two bilingualism questionnaires are interchangeable, the latent overlap between all seven questionnaires suggests that, at the conceptual level, they capture shared aspects of bilingual experience.
